newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Cardoso faces reform tests before re-election bid.
newsitem.headline: Cardoso faces reform tests before re-election bid.

text.p: The way is clear for Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to run for re-election next year, but he still faces a battle to get key reforms through an increasingly unpredictable Congress, analysts said Thursday.
"The difficulties are not going to stop overnight," said political consultant Murillo Aragao. "Just because re-election has been approved doesn't mean everything is perfect."

After a dismal few months marked by infighting among government allies, an alleged corruption scandal, a high-profile demonstration by the radical Landless Movement and a slump in his popularity, Cardoso enjoyed a successful day on Wednesday.

As well as final Senate approval for a constitutional amendment allowing him to stand in the 1998 presidential elections, international investors showed their confidence in Brazil by flocking to a bond swap deal.

And the privatization of the telecommunications sector took a big step forward when a first B Band cellular contract was awarded to a private group. "Three victories for the government," chimed a front-page headline in Jornal do Brasil.
Cardoso was also able to get Luis Eduardo Magalhaes, one of the most influential members of the Chamber of Deputies, to serve as chief whip in the lower house of Congress.

Magalhaes helped secure approval of several key reforms as president of the Chamber of Deputies between 1995 and February this year. He can also call on the clout of his father, Senator Antonio Carlos Magalhaes, a powerful political boss.
Luis Eduardo wasted no time getting back to business, receiving disgruntled lawmakers Wednesday to hear their gripes and note down their demands, newspapers said.

Brasilia-watchers have attributed the government's recent problems in Congress to its failure to come up with pork promised to members of the Chamber of Deputies when the re-election bill was in the lower house.

Magalhaes' first test comes next week when the government hopes to resume voting on amendments to its civil service reform bill, which has run into widespread opposition and has been effectively stalled in the lower house for two months.
He must also persuade deputies to vote for a constitutional amendment that extends the FEF fiscal fund beyond its current June 30 expiry date.

The fund allows the federal government to retain monies earmarked in the constitution for spending by states and municipalities and is considered an important tool in its attempts to rein in public spending. But it is resented by state governors and mayors whose influence over Congress is strong.
"There's no such thing as magic," Magalhaes told daily O Estado de Sao Paulo. "I'm not promising anything because this Congress is not reform-minded. It's conservative."

Analyst Aragao said that while the government might manage to get its civil service bill fully approved in Congress by September, its cut-off date for reforms, its pension reform bill might have to wait until after the elections next year.

The pension bill was awaiting a first reading in the Senate where it has been rewritten to include points lost during lower house voting last year. It will have to return to the Chamber of Deputies for approval of the changes.

Political consultant Paulo Kramer noted that the final approval of the re-election bill marked the beginning of the 1998 election campaign which, for the time being, has only one serious candidate: Cardoso.
But he added that a dark horse winner could not be ruled out.

"Don't forget that a year and a half before the last election, no one imagined Fernando Henrique would be president and Fernando Collor (who won the 1989 presidential election) was a surprise too," Kramer said.
